segments.description: The Adaptive Tennis Program has been running for many years at City Community Tennis. We have up to 22 players that can attend on a Saturday at one time, but it includes anyone with any type of disability. Hi, I'm Joanna Garvin and I've been playing tennis for about two years with Community Tennis. I love coming out here on the court and meeting new people. It's a really inclusive atmosphere here, which is so different, I think, in your day-to-day life in terms of really boosting your confidence. Hi, my name is Monty from the City Community Tennis Adaptive Tennis. I played with the blind and low vision tennis world today. We received the ATP Cup Legacy Fund for our blind, low vision and deaf tennis players. The actual investment has helped towards getting these players to come on. We've run come and try days out of it. We've actually been able to make our website accessible so people who are blind or low vision can actually now go and book a court. It's also helped us invest in the blind low vision tennis balls so that we could actually deliver a blind low vision tennis program. It's given me back my love of tennis. I forgot how much I enjoyed it. Getting new friendships. It's a really fun, safe environment, but we've also got top-class coaching. Hello, my name's Keegan Ochi. I'm a coach here at City Community Tennis. Greatly supported by Tennis New South Wales, Tennis Australia. I really do love being able to coach a bit

and get out on court and enjoy the fresh air and see the next gen come through. Increased funding will allow programs like this to grow and expand and offer the services to a wider group of people. We can see that the program's really growing and welcoming people of all different abilities. So it's really exciting. I would just like to begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the various lands on which everybody's joining us on today. I am here in Sydney and I'm on the traditional lands of the Tungago people and I would like to pay my respects to their elders past, present and emerging and also pass those respects to the various elders of the lands which you're all on and also acknowledge any Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people present today. So I just wanted to firstly introduce myself. My name is Nikita Sayle and I am the Head of Inclusion, Diversity and Programming here at Tennis New South Wales and it's my absolute pleasure to have a very special guest join us, which is Merida Morgan. She is the Facility and Inclusion Manager at City Community Tennis here in Sydney who do some fantastic work in disability and adaptive tennis as we like to call it. So firstly, welcome Merida. Thank you. I'm so happy that you're here to join us and I think that this is a really great opportunity for all the coaches who are going to be watching this around the country to learn a little

bit more about adaptive tennis and the great work that you and the team at City Community Tennis do. So let's dive right in. I think I first wanted to ask you a little bit about how you first got into tennis and I guess what your journey has been. Okay, so I started tennis at a young age. It was actually during school. It was the only sport that I felt that could be inclusive to me other than swimming and swimming was a massive part of my life outside of school. So I got involved at school at Tennis and it was part of the Friday programs at Parklands here in Sydney, Moorpark and then I went to school holiday camps in Snake Park Tennis Courts as well and I was actually coached by Steve Ashcroft for a couple of years at Moorpark and then I stopped tennis because it just got too difficult for me. Running was not always easy and I decided to pursue my other sporting interests in swimming and then when I was older, so in 2018, I had surgery on my right side and that was where I discovered with the excess physiologists from several quality alliance that there was a wheelchair tennis program and you didn't need to be in a wheelchair to play tennis, something I didn't know before this. So I went along to Alexandria here at City Community Tennis, Alexandria Courts, where I met Jerry Majoka and started to play wheelchair tennis at the then called wheelchair tennis development hub and from there it's been a major part of my life

now. I now work at the Tennis Centre. I'm now one of the facility managers. I play in the ITF tournaments. I play in Nationals and yeah, I just love it. That's awesome and Jerry's fantastic as well. We had him come and deliver some adaptive tennis at our future leaders program a couple of years ago now but yeah, he's awesome. That's great and so can you tell us I guess a little bit about the programs that City Community Tennis offers, I guess more broadly and then also the adaptive tennis program? Okay, so City Community Tennis here in Sydney, we have a couple of locations within the City of Sydney area and we run our standard tennis programs such as the Adler Group classes, the Hot Chots, but we've also reached out to other programs and a range of inclusive programs from our Mums on Monday program to Indigenous programs. We work with the settlement to our Buckhouse Mental Health program which has been running for over 20 years and now our adaptive tennis program for anyone with a disability to play tennis. And your team is also is always so fantastic to work with. We've partnered in the First Nation space and yeah, it's been awesome to work with such a diverse team as well which I think is one of your strengths at City Community Tennis but just I think always so open-minded and willing to get involved in any community opportunity just putting your hand up to take it. So in terms of the adaptive tennis program, I guess firstly let's just give everybody maybe a

little bit of understanding about the concept of adaptive tennis and then I might have a one or two other questions for you in terms of the current program. So the adaptive program as I stated before was originally called the wheelchair tennis development hub which receives support from tennis Australia. After being involved in the program for about six months, seven months, I questioned why the program was only for people wanting to learn to play wheelchair tennis and I said that it would be much better to open up the program to anyone with a disability and rename the program to adaptive tennis hub and I guess the word adaptive is used overseas in other countries such as Canada where I was actually part of an adaptive skiing program and saw how inclusive this program was for all people with disabilities. So I suggested to the team at City Community Tennis. While I'm calling it wheelchair tennis, let's call it adaptive tennis so that you're showing that you're adapting to the person's individual needs that you're willing to adapt and include anyone with a disability and it doesn't stigma the word wheelchair. So soon the program grew from five wheelchair tennis players to 15 participants with various disabilities and support needs on the court at the same time. And so what are some of the disabilities I guess that you see in your adaptive programs that you know may not have been included in a wheelchair

tennis program? Autism, acquired brain injury, intellectual disability, blind low vision, deaf, hard of hearing and also people with cerebral palsy that don't necessarily use a day chair and don't want to play in a wheelchair so it gives them the opportunity to play out of the chair and place adaptive stand up tennis. And so I guess when you have people coming to the program you know from your coach's perspective and your perspective as the sort of the program manager it's about people coming as they are and you having the commitment that your team is going to just work with them to adapt what you're delivering to be able to make sure that they're included and and able to participate. Yes and I'm a big part of the person first worry about the disability later so when someone new comes onto the court I won't actually necessarily ask the person what is their disability. I would just ask questions like have you played tennis before, you know what would you like to get out of it and then and that's how I've trained the coaches as well and then as we go on in the morning that's when eventually it will come out what the disability is or what the person's needs are that need to adapt. So yeah so like we had somebody the other week and he's happy for me to share this he turned up and he uses crutches and I just said would you like to play in or out of a chair I think would like to play in a chair it's too hard for me to run played tennis before

in a chair and play tennis so I think from my experience seeing others with cerebral palsy or draws in them struggle to push a wheelchair went on the court I think it's really been necessary to start seeing adaptive tennis be included in these pathways yeah so they may not necessarily be physically able to do it so yeah so in terms of I guess adaptions that would be made with with some of these when we talk about the blind low vision for example could I guess for the coaches who maybe haven't had any experience or you know knowledge of it in the past what what are some of adaptions with these different players that you might so with blind low vision tennis it's they play with a soft foam ball which has got a bell in it and that's what they play off and they hear hear it and then depending on the level of their vision or level of their vision loss depends which category they get put into how many balls that they get to bounce with so like in wheelchair tennis you've got two bounces but in blind low vision it might be one two or three so I think with um with the adaptions for blind low vision it's just having main most important thing is having a um a sound ball available on the court so that when someone comes down and having a smaller racket so in blind low vision tennis you actually use a smaller racket not your standard adult racket it's a kid sized racket that they will play with. Yeah and then I

would also encourage um any coaches who have been approached by um you know people wanting to do blind low vision tennis reach out to your MA or tennis Australia in terms of um equipment and things like that um because those balls aren't always um the easiest to source um and also from across the state they're not always the cheapest but um I'm sure the team at tennis Australia are happy to have those conversations as well and then in terms of um you know when we talk about um stand-up adaptive tennis as you were talking about before that there's people um you know with uh different disabilities who may not um play in a wheelchair but in terms of being able to compete on a full-size court or with standard rules that they may not be able to um compete or play um stand-up would then use I guess different sized courts and and equipment as well. Again it's very it's depending on the level of the disability so yeah from our experience people with um cerebral palsy that we have on the tennis court they all play full-size um full-size courts they get two bounces um if they want to use the two bounces um and then we usually play fast for to manage the um fatigue so we but there are um some categories out there that um will play in orange size um court. Awesome but again it's just about adapting. Yes exactly yeah and I think particularly when you're looking at this yeah we're looking at this from a participation

perspective right so this doesn't have to be you know just because you're in this you know category we're gonna because that's what you might have to do if you went to a competition or something like that you know we're trying to get people playing tennis and so whatever they need to help them play that's what we want to be doing right? Correct um and so in terms of uh people getting into the pathways or getting into playing tennis what are some of the barriers that you see um people come up against? I think it's um lack of awareness um a club not being accessible um a lack of equipment and um sometimes lack of education of people with a disability um you've got to remember that people with disability um sport is often one of the key things that they want to get involved in because then they feel included um and um they might themselves have lack of experience in sport so they're really keen to get involved so I think it's really important um that you just be open-minded and welcome anyone into your club um I think also it's a lack of understanding and awareness of how people have to include people with a disability in sport it's the limited of limited opportunities and programs um quite often it's also um the limited accessible transportation so some people might struggle to get to your club they might not be on a bus line or they might not drive and it's yeah um yeah and what role do you think that you know the coaches I guess watching this

what role can they play in in reducing some of those barriers or making it more accessible for people I think a coach can play a huge part in including players with a disability just being welcoming to players with disability and learning from the player how to adapt to their needs um not judging the person um and looking at the person first is who I've referred to before and coaches advertising that their club is inclusive and inviting for people with a disability I think this is also how you actually um advertise it as well make sure that you know your website is accessible for a person who is um blind or low vision um you know that they can make sure they can read your website um be adaptable for individual um big thing is offer come and try days for people with disabilities uh that's a huge thing if you have a come and try day you might get one person you may get 10 but it's a good starting point um for a coach um and being welcome with people with all disabilities of all ages and not just juniors so if someone who's older that comes to your club with a disability who may never had played sport in their life be welcoming to them as well um and using inclusive language as well um you know but yeah just making the club welcome and if your club is not accessible look at ways to make it accessible reach out to the council or reach out to physical disability Australia and say how can we make our club more accessible

or if you haven't got the equipment like the sports chairs reach out to someone like wheelchair sports in South Wales or disability sports Australia or tennis Australia and say we have a young person in a wheelchair they would like to try tennis can you help us get a wheelchair they're those sorts of things and you don't need to have all the equipment I've seen people just turn up in their day chair and have a hit and they're happy because they're being included yeah absolutely and I also think that one of the big things from I guess you know state sporting organisation perspective is if you don't have the capability or capacity to service somebody at least know where you can refer them I think that for us that's a big thing um I do not want an individual to go to a tennis venue and be told we can't you can't play tennis um I think that yeah at the very least knowing where to be able to refer people is really really important ideally obviously we want to get to a point where coaches are up skilled and facilities are fully accessible and and that that's not not an issue at all but I think where we are currently definitely familiarise yourself with what's going on in your state or in your city where people can access things um so can you tell us a little bit about how you've gone about I guess growing and promoting your programs at City Community Tennis most of the growth of the

City Community Tennis programs whether it's the Adaptive Tennis program the Buckhouse Mental Health program our Indigenous programs has gained through work and health connections that patents will be have built over the years various organisations um you know even just walking up to Redburn station and handing out flyers at some ways that will be used to actually promote the promoting programs um working with Disability Sports Australia and their activation inclusion sports days um they're only recent but they've been a big thing getting involved in them linking in with schools um working with Tennis New South Wales um development officers and reaching out the schools and letting them know that we had this program that's been very helpful um and then I think because I have a lot of connections with the disability set so I've worked for the Sobo-Porsi Alliance I sit on the committee of Sobo-Porsi Sport and Rec so I've been able to work within my networks to promote the programs but even if you don't know a person with a disability don't be afraid to reach out to these organizations and say hey we would like to start something um you know don't be afraid of that and um you know having a connection with the city we have a connection with the Sydney Children's Hospital but you may have a hospital down the road from you know your tennis centre that you can reach out and talk to um and say we

would like to start this program and I think a big thing at the moment is working with the NDIS local area coordinators and that can be challenging but just getting in touch with them and saying you know we've got this program or we're an accessible club we would like to work with with disabilities um and then I guess also we've been fortunate um having a strong connection with um rec link New South Wales as well so yeah so it's mostly working with these um because how we've been able to promote um and word of mouth and people with disabilities talk they talk they talk they talk and parents are big talkers so if you've got parents in the you know the club get them to talk to somebody in the school get them to help you as well so they do talk. That's great advice um you mentioned the NDIS um just a moment ago and and if you're comfortable I'd love to um get your experience as a person who's accessed NDIS but then also how tennis providers can provide support to um participants through the NDIS. Okay so I've been very fortunate I've been on the NDIS um for a few years and um I'm very fortunate cerebral palsy which I have got um it's a disability that's permanent so it's an automatic yes onto the NDIS but it's not always easy for people to get on the NDIS um so I do acknowledge that um I was also involved in the NDIS champion program so that's the program where you went out and spoke about the NDIS and help educate people so I've been able to learn a lot more about the

NDIS um and then I guess I also worked as a youth purchaser for cerebral palsy so I work closely with the NDIS and I have an understanding but I do acknowledge that it can be difficult to navigate and um as a person with disability you really need to fight this sometimes to get something in your plan and unfortunately sport is not always easy to get into the plan because quite often it's just assumed that you're going to get in that sport and you want to be a next Paralympian or you want to become competitive but that's quite often not the reason why people will join in sport um so I think the thing is you've always got to link it back to your disability and your goals um so so for someone to get tennis in the NDIS plan they must show how it benefits them socially how they can gain independence how they can improve their mental and physical well-being and be part of a community um so it's NDIS will not pay for private lessons um so because an able bodied person so can access private lessons themselves so it's it can be difficult to get a private lesson however as many of you will be aware that people with disabilities may not be able to last an hour may not be able to last half an hour so they need to have a one-on-one session or their disability does not allow them to join a group session because they've got other issues or they're not comfortable so they want to start off with private lessons so but sessions such as
